title: Slow to Anger and Fast to Forgive: Cooperation in an Uncertain World

original_source.version_note: Complete original abstract only; full body inaccessible through attempted publisher/author routes.

central_claims: Cooperation is higher when it is an equilibrium despite implementation noise; successful cooperative strategies tolerate initial defections and forgive.

source_manifest.title: Slow to Anger and Fast to Forgive: Cooperation in an Uncertain World
source_manifest.finding: Original central claims were recorded before follow-up grading.

source_manifest.title: Camerer et al. Evaluating replicability of laboratory experiments in economics — Supplement, Tables S1–S2
source_manifest.finding: The preregistered independent comparison tests whether cooperative equilibria raise cooperation under implementation noise; replication N=128, original focal N=124, p=<.001. The project only retested one selected result per paper.

source_manifest.title: Archived preregistered replication protocol
source_manifest.finding: The individual replication team is Colin Camerer and Gidi Nave, distinct from the original authors; this page is a protocol, not a results report.

source_manifest.title: Evaluating replicability of laboratory experiments in economics: supplementary materials, Tables S1–S2
source_manifest.finding: The selected cooperation contrast reproduced: N=128, p<.001, r=.33, versus original N=124 and r=.30. Table S2 identifies the benefit/cost 1.5 versus 2 contrast. Independent data collection was led by Camerer and Nave; the consortium also includes original coauthor Dreber.

source_manifest.title: Fast to Forgive, Slow to Retaliate: Intuitive Responses in the Ultimatum Game Depend on the Degree of Unfairness
source_manifest.finding: Ferguson and colleagues explicitly integrate the original uncertainty/forgiveness idea into a hypothesis about unfair offers, testing it in ultimatum games. Mildly unfair offers elicited more acceptance with shorter delays.

source_manifest.title: Individual versus group choices of repeated game strategies: A strategy method approach
source_manifest.finding: Cason and Mui use the original parameters and twenty strategies for direct choices by individuals and groups. They identify group differences in forgiveness and persistent poor-performing defection. Publisher abstract, introduction and section excerpts were read; institutional metadata confirms March 2019.

source_manifest.title: Fudenberg et al. replication protocol
source_manifest.finding: The protocol names Camerer and Nave, a Claremont sample, original software and predefined analysis. This is a plan, not the final results table.

search_gaps: This is a complete but selected cohort of laboratory economics experiments, not a representative sample of research success.
The replication project tests only one selected comparison, not every claim or the entire theoretical contribution.
Outcome review prioritizes independently tested validation; absent adoption/utility evidence remains unknown.
Original assessment uses its complete abstract only; attempted full-text publisher/author routes were inaccessible. No fabricated full-text reading.

An original coauthor participated in the overall multi-paper project; the named team running this individual replication had different authors (Camerer/Nave for Fudenberg; Dreber/Isaksson/Johannesson for Kirchler), as documented by the archived protocol.
Two independent grades adjudicated; six-paper repeat sample is not a population reliability estimate.
research.summary: The independent preregistered replication supported the focal result that cooperative equilibria raise cooperation under implementation noise (p=<.001, N=128). This judgment is restricted to that central component; it does not validate all other claims. Broader uptake, application and long-term dominance are not inferred from replication alone. Blind repeat research added sources and corrected claim scope; initial and repeat grades remain archived.
